items.text: Think more rain means more river water? Not necessarily
items.article: Some rivers are receiving more rain than before but have lower water flow, according to a study More rain and snow equals more water in rivers, right? Not necessarily. A new study shows that, despite receiving more rainfall than they used to, river water levels are falling because of changes in climate. Global heating is intensifying the hydrological cycle, making wet regions wetter and dry regions drier, but how is this affecting river flow? Researchers from the Pennsylvania State University, in the US, have analysed precipitation and river flow records in more than 10,000 rivers between 1951 and 2020. In nearly one-third of rivers, they found that flow trends did not match with the changes observed in rainfall and snow. The findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters , show that more than 10% of rivers receive more precipitation now than they did 50 years ago but have lower rates of flow. This mismatch appears to be more common in regions where rainfall extremes are becoming more common, and where evaporation rates are high. Rivers and freshwater lakes play a vital role in supporting human life, with large cities obtaining nearly 80% of their water from surface water sources. This research highlights the need to understand the other factors that control river flow, and monitor trends in river discharge rates, as well as precipitation, to predict future water availability in a changing climate.

items.article: How much protein do you really need each day? Dt Amreen Sheikh explains the daily protein requirement, how to calculate it and easy food sources. Protein has become a major focus in conversations about fitness, weight management, and healthy ageing. But how much do you actually need every day? And does everyone need the same amount? According to Dt Amreen Sheikh, Chief Dietician, KIMS Hospitals, Thane, protein requirements are primarily calculated based on body weight, but several other factors can influence an individual’s needs. “For a healthy adult, the ICMR-NIN recommendation is about 0.83 g of protein per kg of body weight each day,” said Sheikh. For example, a person weighing 60 kg would need approximately 50 g of protein a day based on this recommendation. However, this is not a one-size-fits-all number. “Factors such as age, body weight, level of physical activity and life stage can affect personal protein needs,” Sheikh explained. People who exercise regularly, older adults and those trying to preserve muscle mass may require more protein than a sedentary adult. items.article: Aparna Nair, IBM's chief talent officer, says college students and entry-level workers need these two skills to succeed as AI reshapes their work. As AI reshapes how people work, particularly along the lowest rungs of the career ladder , many college students and entry-level workers are left wondering what skills will carry them furthest. Two skills in particular are important to develop right now, if you ask Aparna Nair, IBM's chief talent, leadership & culture officer. Entry-level workers "have to be focused on ensuring that they are actually building critical thinking [and] judgment," Nair tells CNBC Make It. "There are some things that are going to rapidly change, and some things that humans, only, can do today, which is where they need to double down." In an IBM survey of 1,500 chief human resources officers and 8,800 employees worldwide published in September, roughly 57% of CHROs considered critical thinking an important skill in the AI era, compared to 49% of employees. Approximately 48% of CHROs consider judgment under uncertainty and ambiguity an important skill, compared to just 29% of employees. "Traditionally people were building judgment through actually doing the work," Nair says. "Today, that piece of work is no longer there because AI is doing it." Instead, "actually validating the inputs of AI," Nair says, "helps them build their judgment."

Working long hours may seem like part of building a successful company, but former Meta executive Martin Ott says his time working with Mark Zuckerberg taught him a different approach. Ott, who is now the CEO of Berlin-based tax platform Taxfix, says leaders should focus on the work that matters most instead of trying to stay busy all day. Taxfix is valued at more than $1 billion. Ott joined Facebook in 2012 as managing director for Northern and Central Europe. The company was still private at the time and was moving from desktop use to mobile, with only a few thousand employees around the world. Speaking to Fortune, Ott said one of the key lessons he took from working under Zuckerberg was that time is limited and should be used carefully. “There’s only so many hours in a day," Ott said. According to Ott, spending more hours at work does not always mean creating more value.
